 Be a better Philadelphia citizen
 One of the founding tenets of The Philadelphia Citizen is to get people  the resources they need  to become better, more engaged citizens of their city.
 We hope to do that in our Good Citizenship Toolkit, which includes a host of ways to get involved in Philadelphia — whether you want to  contact your City Councilmember  to voice your support for small businesses, get those experiencing  homelessness the goods they need , or simply  go out to dinner somewhere  where you know your money is going toward a greater good.
 Find an issue that’s important to you in the list below, and get started on your journey of A-plus citizenship.
 Vote and strengthen democracy 
 Stand up for marginalized communities 
 Create a cleaner, greener Philadelphia 
 Help our local youth and schools succeed

 Guest Commentary An Election Day Love Letter to Philadelphia
 A local resident was scared about what might happen at the polls. What she experienced as an election observer was not what she expected
 BY Laura Bellet 
 Nov. 05, 2026 
 I volunteered as an election observer out of fear and trepidation. Bad stuff — ICE presence, in particular — wasn’t out of the question. But I was well-trained, ready to record incidents and answer questions, and poised to reach out for help if needed. 
 What I didn’t anticipate was a six-hour stint that would underscore everything I love about this city. The worst failed to materialize. The best prevailed. 
 If a polling place is a microcosm of a city, this North Philadelphia neighborhood did itself proud. The poll workers were experienced, welcoming, and kind. They included a college student, an entrepreneur and a brother and sister of retirement age. 
 They could easily field any voter question. “Where does the paper ballot go?” Let me show you. “Oh no. I’m at the wrong polling place.” Let’s check and see where you are listed. “Can my son go in the voting booth with me?” Sure. 
 My role was more or less extraneous. I ended up perching on a chair near the door, greeting voters as they arrived and thanking them for voting as they departed. I felt more like a hostess than a keeper of democracy. It was a big relief. 
 The worst failed to materialize. The best prevailed. 
 Nonetheless, I was determined to finish my shift, even if my role was less than mission-critical. So I leaned into conversation with the polling place team — the kind of exchanges that make strangers into friends, at least for a while. We talked about kids and grand kids. About sibling rivalry. About racism in the 1960s. About building a business. About legendary family reunions. We cooed over a baby. Phone numbers were exchanged, for possible babysitting, for a future internship. Photos of pets were shared. 
 Did we discuss politics or the uneasy state of the union? No, it wasn’t the place. Did we, by happenstance, manifest the strength of democracy in action? Absolutely. It felt like a given, as a steady stream of citizens showed up to do their civic duty. 
 Then, after the final voter rushed in at 7:59, it was time to go. I logged out of the election observer app on my phone, said my goodbyes, and walked home. 
 Philadelphia is a beautiful, troubled city. I am proud to call it home. And the next time someone asks me about living here, I’ll share this story. It says it all. 
 Laura G. Bellet lives in Philadelphia. 
 The Citizen welcomes guest commentary from community members who represent that it is their own work and their own opinion based on true facts that they know firsthand.
